newsitem.title: VATICAN: Vatican newspaper slams U.S. judges over execution.
newsitem.headline: Vatican newspaper slams U.S. judges over execution.

text.p: The Vatican's newspaper slammed U.S. judges on Wednesday for failing to suspend the planned execution of a man convicted of murder and rape, despite what it called "irrefutable evidence" of his innocence.

In an editorial entitled "When Legalism Prevails Over Justice," L'Osservatore Romano said the fate of Joseph O'Dell, due to be executed in Virginia on December 18, had been decided on technical grounds rather than evidence that has emerged since his trial.
It was written by Vatican moral theologian Gino Concetti, who is considered close to Pope John Paul.

Citing newspaper reports, Concetti said judges had ruled against suspending the execution because "the evidence was not presented (to the court) within 21 days of the sentencing, as local law required".
He said DNA testing had proven O'Dell's innocence, adding that his chief accuser had retracted testimony against the 55-year-old, who has spent 12 years in a Virginia prison.
"It's worth wondering if the expiration of a deadline for the presentation of evidence is a just motive for not stopping an execution and 'reviewing' the entire trial," Concetti said.
He urged judges "to seek to reconcile civil rights with the requirements of justice, without committing further injustices or taking recourse to iniquitous measures".

O'Dell was convicted in 1985 of the murder of Helen Schartner and sentenced to death. Evidence subsequent to his trial based on DNA testing showed blood found on his shirt did not match that of the victim, according to published reports.
O'Dell's case has received considerable publicity in Italy, where the rights group Amnesty International has scheduled a demonstration on Thursday in front of the U.S. embassy in Rome.
In an encyclical last year, the Pope brought the Roman Catholic Church the closest it has come to calling for a total ban on capital punishment, allowed by 38 U.S. states in murder cases.
The Pope acknowledged traditional Church teaching that allows capital punishment in extremely rare cases, but said such cases were practically non-existent in modern society.
